channel: Oil volumes and prices (conditional on security)
direction: Positive only if output rises clearly above the 2026 average; roughly unchanged if disruption persists at 2026 intensity; negative if it worsens
quantified: Illustrative, our assumptions, not a forecast, on one output series (OPEC secondary sources, E-037): 2026 averages about 8.2 mb/d (Q1 9.33, Q2 6.82, Q3 7.52; Q4 assumed at the October 9.19). Holding the October level through 2027 is about +12%; the 10.48 mb/d OPEC+ required level about +28%. With Brent moving from EIA's 2026 estimate of USD 97.4 to its 2027 forecast of USD 85.8 (−12%, E-040), crude export revenue would change by roughly −2% to +12% against full-year 2026. Break-even output at that price is about 9.3 mb/d. The MoF's 'crude oil supply' of 7.9 mb/d for Jan–Sep 2026 is a different series and is not mixed in.
rationale: The final budget's growth path assumes oil output recovers: real GDP +10.9% in 2027 after −2.1% in 2026, with oil activity −14.6% through Q3 2026. The Minister says higher Q4 output has already raised the 2026 comparison base. Against full-year 2026, a recovery that lifts output clearly above about 9.3 mb/d is net positive for sector revenue even with lower prices. If the disruption persists at 2026 intensity, 2027 roughly repeats 2026 (higher prices, lower volumes). Only a worsening, such as further damage to facilities or export routes, is clearly negative. Tankers were hit in Hormuz on 21 and 25 Nov.
depends_on_execution: Hormuz and Red Sea security; OPEC+ 2027 levels (29 Nov 2026)
indicators_to_watch: Monthly Saudi output (one series); Brent; OPEC+ decision; Hormuz traffic

channel: Volumes, prices and export capacity
quantified: Historical context (not a policy effect): 9M 2026 realised crude price +29.2% and liquids output −15.2% (Aramco 9M 2026 interim report, key figures p.1 and production p.6; revenue in fact 2222-9M2026-REV). The budget gives no 2027 oil-revenue assumption.
rationale: Aramco carries almost all of the sector's oil price and volume exposure. A plan to raise East-West Pipeline throughput to about 10 mb/d is under consideration, with preliminary engineering and no final investment decision. If built, it would cut reliance on Hormuz but add capex. Its revenue effect is not determinable.
depends_on_execution: EWP expansion is under consideration (no FID); 2027 oil revenue not published
indicators_to_watch: Aramco FY2026 results; EWP FID

channel: Government funding needs, dividends, PIF and share sales
quantified: Historical context: Aramco's 2025 distributions of SAR 320.4bn equalled its free cash flow (company-reported; matches fact 2222-FY2025-FCF).
rationale: The deficit (SAR 190.6bn) and financing costs (+31.1% to SAR 93bn) keep the state and PIF reliant on Aramco's base dividend, which has recently risen 3.5% a year. The Minister's move to a National Privatization Strategy (about 202 projects) keeps government share sales open as a financing option; the last Aramco offering was in Jun 2024. Aramco agreed with PIF to take 49% of HUMAIN (PIF-owned), contributing SAR 9.9bn of cash to HUMAIN plus certain AI assets (9M 2026 interim report), which shows PIF using Aramco's balance sheet for its own projects. No change to Aramco's dividend or any share sale has been announced.
risks: Payout pressure alongside USD 50–55bn capex; share-sale overhang
indicators_to_watch: Aramco dividend declarations; privatisation announcements

channel: Domestic energy prices and subsidies
direction: Neutral / not determinable until the Jan 2027 price notices
quantified: Not quantified. Total subsidies fall 61.6% (SAR 48bn to 18bn), mainly support to electricity and water companies.
rationale: The budget changes electricity and water tariffs only. Aramco's regulated fuel and feedstock prices are set separately, and no 2027 change is confirmed. Any increase would raise Aramco's domestic revenue but reduce its price-equalisation income from the government. The budget does not say whether lower utility subsidies change the fuel prices charged to the power sector.
indicators_to_watch: Annual price notices; other income related to sales

channel: Freight rates, Aramco volumes and security
direction: Negative vs 2026 if flows normalise; holds up if disruption persists
quantified: Historical context: Bahri 9M 2026 revenue SAR 26.1bn vs 7.1bn (facts 4030-9M2026-REV, 4030-9M2025-REV); VLCC rates above USD 1m/day in Sep 2026.
rationale: Bahri's 2026 surge came from crisis freight rates and Aramco's rerouted exports. Normalisation would bring more cargo but lower rates, and rates would dominate. The government marine-insurance pool is described as cutting insurance costs on shipments arriving at Saudi ports. There is no evidence that it covers Bahri's export tankers, so it is not counted as support here. Security risk is company-specific: the Houthi blockade of Saudi shipping, the attack on the tanker AMZAN, and tankers hit in Nov 2026. If the disruption persists at 2026 intensity, crisis rates and rerouted Aramco cargoes are likely to continue, so persistence is the better case for Bahri relative to normalisation.
indicators_to_watch: VLCC TCE rates; Bahri Q4 2026; Red Sea and Hormuz incidents

channel: Refining margins, feedstock prices, Zakat and shareholder support
direction: Negative vs 2026 if supply normalises; holds up if disruption persists
quantified: Historical context: Petro Rabigh 9M 2026 net profit SAR 6.7bn vs a SAR 3.3bn loss (facts 2380-9M2026-NI_ATTR, 2380-9M2025-NI_ATTR). Tariff effect not quantified.
rationale: The 2026 profit came from crisis refining margins, which are not a budget item and are likely to narrow as supply normalises. Feedstock price notices (each January) and Zakat on a now-profitable base are more direct cost channels than the electricity tariff. Petro Rabigh's own utility supply arrangements have not been verified. Aramco, with about 60%, remains the funding backstop. If the disruption persists, crisis refining margins are likely to persist too. Top-up tax: Petro Rabigh's 9M 2026 zakat and tax was SAR 0.41bn on pre-tax profit of SAR 7.1bn (5.8%; 9M 2026 interim, statement of profit or loss). Aramco equity-accounts it as an associate (FY2025 AFS) but holds about 60%, and under the OECD model rules an equity-accounted entity at least 50% owned by the group is treated as a joint venture and included in the top-up calculation. Petro Rabigh is therefore the most exposed company in the sector if the Saudi rules follow the model and Zakat does not count as a covered tax (see P-E-10).
indicators_to_watch: Product cracks; Petro Rabigh Q4 2026

channel: Upstream activity, geographic mix and acquisition debt
quantified: Historical context: 9M 2026 finance costs SAR 976m vs 668m, driven by borrowings that rose to about SAR 20bn after the Shelf Drilling acquisition, not by policy rates.
rationale: Restored Saudi output and the gas programme support rig demand. Maximum sustainable capacity is held at 12 mb/d, which limits new oil-capacity drilling. ADES differs from Arabian Drilling because it is now diversified beyond Saudi Arabia through Shelf, so it is less exposed to Saudi suspensions but carries more acquisition debt. Its Saudi segment revenue fell 12.8% in FY2025 and 13.1% in 9M 2026. The acquisition of Saudi Arabian Saipem (15 Sep 2026: 3 owned and 2 leased premium jack-ups with customer contracts, SAR 1,133.9m) adds Saudi exposure back. The rate channel is minor next to its own leverage.
indicators_to_watch: Aramco rig resumptions; ADES backlog

channel: Rig activity and refinancing
direction: Mixed (activity guided to recover; refinancing risk is company-specific)
quantified: Historical context: 9M 2026 revenue SAR 2,397m vs 2,609m (−8.1%); attributable profit SAR 6.9m vs 73.3m. Company-specific risk, outside the policy rating: SAR 2bn sukuk due 3 Feb 2027, covenant waiver to 31 Mar 2027, current liabilities above current assets by about SAR 1.6bn (company filings).
rationale: Policy link: rig activity follows Aramco's upstream programme, which the budget's output recovery assumes. Arabian Drilling received notices in Aug 2026 to resume all remaining suspended offshore rigs and guided full offshore utilisation by end-Q3 2026; the recovery is guided but not yet visible in 9M 2026 results. The refinancing of the Feb 2027 sukuk is a company risk in tighter funding conditions; its link to government borrowing is indirect.
indicators_to_watch: Refinancing announcement; rig utilisation

channel: Equity-market exposure
quantified: Not quantified.
rationale: SARCO's results depend on dividends and its listed-share portfolio. It has no direct budget channel.
indicators_to_watch: TASI

channel: Corporate tax: Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (from 1 Jan 2027)
direction: Negative for in-scope groups with a low Saudi effective rate
quantified: Not quantified: the detailed rules, including whether Zakat counts as a covered tax, have not been reviewed. First ranking from our data (zakat and tax ÷ pre-tax profit): Aramco 50% (FY2025), ADES 20% (FY2025), Petro Rabigh 6% (9M 2026), Bahri 2–5% (FY2024–9M 2026).
rationale: A domestic top-up tax is collected in the Kingdom on the Saudi profits of multinational groups with consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750m in two of the four preceding years (press report of ZATCA's announcement); purely domestic groups without foreign entities are excluded. Aramco's Saudi income already bears income tax well above 15%. Petro Rabigh is the most exposed (about 60% Aramco-owned and equity-accounted, so caught by the joint-venture rule; see P-E-06). Bahri is above the revenue threshold, but international shipping income is excluded from the model rules' tax base, so its exposure depends on its other income. ADES's group rate is above 15%. Whether Bahri and Arabian Drilling count as multinational groups (foreign entities) has not been verified; SARCO is below the threshold. No Zakat rule change for 2027 was found (search to 26 Nov 2026).
risks: Higher effective tax for low-taxed entities
indicators_to_watch: ZATCA regulations

channel: Government borrowing, deposits and bank liquidity
quantified: Gross domestic borrowing in 9M 2026 was SAR 235bn, about 7.7% of bank deposits (SAR 3,076bn); net of domestic repayments about SAR 193bn (6.3%). How much banks absorbed is not disclosed. 2027 net borrowing need: debt +SAR 190bn in the budget, against +SAR 214bn in the budget's 2026 estimate; that 2026 estimate understates 2026, because the 2026 deficit was SAR 245bn and debt had already risen SAR 255bn by end-Q3 (F-048, F-079).
rationale: The final Budget Statement states an intention for 2027 borrowing to 'focus on domestic and private market channels'; the size and mix await the NDMC 2027 plan. The 2027 need is smaller than 2026's. Funding is already tight: Fitch reports tighter and more expensive funding, and government-entity deposits at SAMA near a five-year low (about SAR 370bn on Fitch's measure; the budget's 'government reserves at SAMA' of SAR 399bn is a different measure). Time deposits now exceed demand deposits. On the simple ratio, loans exceed deposits (107% at 30 Sep 2026), but SAMA's regulatory ratio is below 85% at all ten banks against a 90% cap. That means wholesale-funding reliance rather than a binding limit. J.P. Morgan index inclusion of SAR sukuk from 29 Jan 2027 should add foreign demand. Partly offsetting: higher oil revenue, if spent, adds to bank deposits (Fitch).
indicators_to_watch: NDMC plan; SAR sukuk auctions; 3M SAIBOR; time-deposit share

channel: Government spending, projects, PIF and utilities lending
direction: Neutral to slightly negative vs the 2022–25 trend
quantified: Loan growth was 12.3% a year in 2022–25, then +6.4% y/y for listed-bank loans to Sep 2026. Fitch expects about 8% sector credit growth in 2027.
rationale: 2027 spending is 3% below the 2026 estimated outturn, but 6% above the FY2026 budget, and capex is 10% above the FY2026 budget. The Ministry of Finance attributes the −2.1% capex change mainly to military spending brought forward into 2026, not to civil project cuts. Project rescheduling is a stated signal without a list. Two further channels: PIF and government-related entities are large bank borrowers, so their project choices reach banks directly. Lower utility subsidies change the cash needs of the power and water companies, a fast-growing bank exposure. Loan growth should stay well below the 2022–25 pace, but roughly flat to slightly higher than in 2026.
indicators_to_watch: Quarterly budget capex; credit growth by sector

channel: Contractor payments
quantified: Not quantified.
rationale: The amended Government Tenders and Procurement Law bars a government entity from awarding new contracts if it has not addressed outstanding payments, as set out in the Implementing Regulations. If enforced, it should reduce payment delays to contractors, a recurring source of corporate credit stress.
indicators_to_watch: Corporate impairments; contractor receivables

channel: Interest rates (Sep 2026 +25 bp)
quantified: Observed margin response (net special commission income ÷ average assets): in the 2023 hiking year it rose at Riyad (2.93%→3.33%), SAB (2.52%→3.08%), ANB (2.78%→3.35%), BSF (2.87%→3.23%), Alinma (3.24%→3.50%) and SAIB (2.70%→2.86%), and fell at Al Rajhi (3.20%→2.71%), Bank Aljazira (2.38%→1.94%), Albilad (3.23%→3.01%) and SNB (2.83%→2.72%).
rationale: Observed bank by bank, not a fixed- versus floating-rate rule. In the 2023 hiking year margins rose at Riyad, SAB, ANB, BSF, Alinma and SAIB and fell at Al Rajhi, Aljazira, Albilad and SNB; that change also reflects the lagged repricing of about 400 bp of 2022 hikes. In the 2024–25 cuts (FY2023 to FY2025) margins fell at Riyad (3.33%→2.69%), SAB (3.08%→2.72%), ANB (3.35%→3.05%), BSF (3.23%→2.89%), Alinma (3.50%→3.19%), SAIB (2.86%→2.14%), SNB (2.72%→2.52%) and Albilad (3.01%→2.90%), were flat at Aljazira (1.94%→1.90%) and recovered only at Al Rajhi (2.71%→2.96%; 3.19% annualised in 9M 2026). Without disclosed repricing-gap data the direction for each bank is uncertain, and a single 25 bp rise is small either way. SAMA follows the US Federal Reserve under the peg.
indicators_to_watch: SAMA decisions; 3M SAIBOR

channel: Household incomes, tariffs and retail credit
quantified: New residential mortgages: 2025 −12%, then stabilising in 2026 (Aug SAR 5.87bn, flat y/y).
rationale: Several confirmed measures support household income: SANED wage support, the Citizen Account extended to end-2027, the SAR 500 monthly allowance increase and higher Nitaqat wage floors (SAR 5,000 then 6,000). These support salary-based retail lending. The 2027 electricity and water tariffs raise household costs. Mortgage demand has stabilised after the 2025 fall. Retail-heavy banks are most exposed in both directions.
indicators_to_watch: Monthly mortgages; retail impairments

channel: Capital rules (countercyclical buffer)
quantified: 1% countercyclical buffer in effect since 25 May 2026 (measure confirmed).
rationale: The buffer must be met with common equity, so it is met mainly through retained earnings and lower payouts; Tier 1 sukuk do not count towards it. Banks' heavy AT1 issuance in 2026 (about SAR 34.5bn of sukuk, mostly AT1) raises Tier 1 ratios and funds growth. Its coupons reduce returns to ordinary shareholders, which our ROE already deducts.
indicators_to_watch: CET1 ratios; dividend payouts

channel: Corporate tax: Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax
direction: Negative for in-scope banks if Zakat is not a covered tax; small or nil if it is
significance: Not determinable (illustration: up to about 5% of pre-tax profit for a bank at a 10% rate)
quantified: Illustrative upper bound, our arithmetic, not a forecast. Zakat and tax were 10.2–15.7% of pre-tax profit in FY2025 (Al Rajhi 10.2%, SNB 10.4%, Riyad 10.3%, SAB 12.9%, Alinma 10.2%, BSF 10.6%, ANB 14.5%, Albilad 10.3%, SAIB 14.4%, Aljazira 15.7%). If a 15% minimum applied on that base and none of the Zakat counted, a bank at 10.2% would pay about 4.8% of pre-tax profit more (Al Rajhi: about SAR 1.3bn on FY2025 pre-tax profit of SAR 27.6bn). The model rules' tax base and covered taxes differ from these accounting figures, so this is an order of magnitude only.
rationale: A domestic minimum top-up tax is collected in the Kingdom on the Saudi-located profits of in-scope multinational groups. It does not reach foreign subsidiaries, whose host countries mostly tax banks above 15% (e.g. Türkiye, Pakistan, Jordan, Malaysia). A bank is in scope only if its group has foreign entities and revenue of at least EUR 750m in two of the four preceding years. SNB and Al Rajhi have foreign subsidiaries or branches; the other banks' foreign presence has not been verified. The size of any top-up depends mainly on whether Zakat counts as a covered tax under the Saudi rules, which have not been reviewed.
indicators_to_watch: ZATCA regulations

channel: Security escalation and credit quality
quantified: 9M 2026 sector impairments +18.3% (SAR 6,820m vs 5,766m), but concentrated: Al Rajhi +SAR 670m of the +SAR 1,053m (64%), while SNB's charge was SAR 2.6m. Impairments on financing alone rose 12.8%. Sector impairments fell in each year FY2023–FY2025.
rationale: Several banks report a significant escalation after 30 Sep 2026 as a subsequent event; Al Rajhi and SNB state no material ECL impact from the conflict so far. The budget's base case assumes recovery. If disruption persists, credit costs are likely to rise; the filings do not show which segments would be most affected.

channel: Labour costs: Nitaqat wage floors
direction: Negative (small) for employers of lower-paid Saudi staff
quantified: Not quantified: the filings do not disclose wage distributions.
rationale: The minimum wage that earns full Nitaqat credit rises to SAR 5,000 six months after the measures start and to SAR 6,000 twelve months later. Employers with Saudi staff paid below those levels face higher costs or lower Nitaqat credit: drillers' field crews, Bahri's onshore staff and banks' branch and call-centre staff are the likely groups. The same measure supports household incomes (P-B-05).
